explanation: Diffuse: fires on assorted tokens in code (identifiers, #define, comment openers, type keywords), in CJK/multibyte byte fragments, and on spaces before numbers in prose; no shared token or context, with weak scattered activation on ordinary function words.

Mixed: fires on boilerplate/structural tokens at the start of files or pages (header extensions like '.h' in #include lists, '/**' and ' *' doc-comment openers, 'Category:' metadata, breadcrumb '»'), plus mid-word subword pieces of technical terms (ocyte, ro, erm, pan); the top example 'You will hear from us soon' is an outlier.

Fires on a piece in the middle of a fixed, memorized string where the rest can be predicted: digits inside error/product codes (C2061, C57, S7-300, hex colors), inner subwords of proper names (Tenzing, Stengel, Udzungwa), and words inside standard license boilerplate ('OF ANY KIND', 'Use of this software', 'notice,'). The common thread is predictable continuation inside a memorized sequence.

Fires on a person's name (often the second subword of a surname) when it comes back as a later mention of someone already introduced in the text (K-ieran, Razz-az, St-uber, Kimmel). Second job: the tag name in HTML closing tags after '</' (table, ul, a, select). Acronym pieces and plain words fire weakly.

Fires mainly on code syntax tokens: C# property accessors 'get'/'set' inside '{ get; set; }', 'require('' in JS, '=' assignments in MATLAB, 'void'/'extern' type keywords, method calls like '.get'/'countDocuments'. It also fires on Arabic religious words (Allah, Allahu) and a few odd subwords, which form an unrelated offshoot.

Fires on the separator right before the year in a date (the space after 'April 5,' or 'Apr 12', or '-'/'/' in numeric dates), strongest where a 4-digit year follows a month and day, as in post dates and tweet timestamps. Weaker on spaces or separators inside other number formats (case numbers, dimensions).

Fires on tokens inside non-English Romance/Germanic text, especially Portuguese, Spanish, French and German function words (que, você, se, für, Ils) and subwords of foreign words or names. Also fires on all-caps legal text and inner pieces of foreign or technical names. Weak on ordinary English.

Broad: fires on a word that completes a fixed collocation or common phrase, usually a verb particle, preposition or object that is predictable from the verb before it (effectuate, tread on, derived from, jump to, throwing in the towel, revocable, reversed and rendered). Seen across legal, licence, code and web text; weaker on ordinary predictable words.

Fires most strongly on Russian (Cyrillic) words, especially the start of a sentence or word after code or Latin text in Russian Q&A posts (В, по, д-лина, нап-ример). Weaker on English idiom completions ('the same', 'for the life of me', 'that's right', 'God rest') and on Chinese words.

Fires on a mid-word token inside a rare proper noun, a taxon, or a random string (Emperor p-enguins, Cerc-opithecidae, Maine Co-on, Dibrugar-h, base64/ID strings like 'd', 'c', 'h'), plus some legal-formula tokens ('County Court at Law', 'v.') and doc tags ('@var'). The thread is completing an unusual multi-token name or code.

Mixed: fires on 'public'/'private' in key or access contexts (public key, private parts), 'SHALL' in 'IN NO EVENT SHALL' licence text, and assorted subwords inside biomedical or technical compound terms (immun-om-odulatory, activ-ator, -rich, hypers-ensitivity) and place names. Several unrelated triggers.

Fires on tag questions and confirmation tags at the end of a clause: "isn't it", "are you", "haven't", and especially ', right?' asking for agreement. Weaker on 'right' meaning 'just' or 'exactly' ('right now', 'right here'), and very weak on clause-final commas.

Fires on words about religion, spirituality, mythology, the psyche or humanistic culture (mythology, secular, soul, devotional, legends, knowledge, psych-, historic, modern Paganism), plus subword pieces of psychiatric or pharmacological drug names (antipsych-, clonidine, scopolamine, hypnotherapy). Strongest on the topical content word, regardless of syntax.

Fires on mid-word subword pieces inside foreign or transliterated proper names and non-English words (Greek letters, Russian, Finnish, Norwegian, Indian and Turkmen place or person names, Japanese katakana), and on digits inside long numbers or hashes. Common in gazetteer-style articles about places. Ordinary English words do not trigger it.
